model: One-period model: X_0=0, X_1 ~ Cauchy(0,1). F_0 trivial, F_1=sigma(X_1). Dynamic strategies are deterministic constants phi_1 in R. Static payoff set Y = all zero-mean random variables.

dynamic_no_arbitrage.label: dynamic_no_arbitrage
dynamic_no_arbitrage.reasoning: K_0 ∩ L^0_+ = {0}. Proof: X_1 ~ Cauchy(0,1) has full support on R. If phi_1 * X_1 >= 0 a.s., then phi_1 = 0 (since for phi_1 != 0, the event {phi_1 * X_1 < 0} has positive P-measure). Hence the only nonneg element of K_0 is the zero payoff.

semi_static_no_arbitrage.label: semi_static_no_arbitrage
semi_static_no_arbitrage.reasoning: (K_0 + Y) ∩ L^0_+ = {0}. Proof: An element of K_0 + Y has the form a*X_1 + Z where a in R and Z in Y (zero-mean). If a*X_1 + Z >= 0 a.s., then Z = -a*X_1 + W for nonneg W. Since Y is a linear subspace containing zero-mean r.v.s, a constant c >= 0 lies in Y only if c = 0. Any nonneg nonconstant r.v. in L^0_+ has strictly positive expectation under any absolutely-continuous measure, violating E[Z]=0. Therefore the nonneg element must be 0 a.s., proving NA(Y).

pricing_measure_existence.label: pricing_measure_existence
pricing_measure_existence.reasoning: M(Y) = empty set. Proof: Suppose Q ~ P satisfies E_Q[Z] = 0 for all Z in Y (Y is a linear subspace, so the <=0 condition becomes =0). Y contains, for every Borel set A with 0 < P(A) < 1, the r.v. Z_A = 1_A - P(A) (which is zero-mean under P). E_Q[Z_A] = Q(A) - P(A) = 0 for all such A implies Q = P. But Q = P is a martingale measure only if E_P[X_1] = 0, which does not hold for the Cauchy (its expectation is undefined — X_1 is not P-integrable). Alternatively, X_1 itself (or any nonzero scalar multiple) lies in Y if we interpret Y as formal-zero-mean L^0 variables; but requiring Q ~ P to be a martingale measure with Q-integrable X_1 and E_Q[X_1] = 0 is impossible because the Cauchy tails prevent any absolutely-continuous Q from giving X_1 a finite first moment while remaining equivalent to P on the full Borel sigma-algebra. Therefore M(Y) = empty.

conclusion: This model is a COUNTEREXAMPLE to the implication NA(Y) => M(Y) nonempty when Assumption 3.3 is not imposed. NA(Y) = True, M(Y) = empty. The failure arises because Y = all zero-mean r.v.s is too large and violates the small-cone structure required by Assumption 3.3.
warning: The conclusions above are analytic. Monte Carlo illustrations show the Cauchy's heavy tails and empirical-mean instability, but do NOT constitute proofs of theorem validity or invalidity.
